Thermal barrier coatings have been used in gas turbines for over 30 years.
The first application of TBCs was on augmenter liners to provide thermal protection during afterburner operation.
TBCs have been used in diesel engines since the mid-1970s.
The Department of Energy has supported thermal barrier coating development for diesel engine applications.
The primary purpose of thermal barrier coatings in diesel engines is to reduce thermal fatigue.
TBCs can increase the efficiency of diesel engines by reducing heat losses.
The typical thickness of a TBC system is around 100-200 microns.
The expected lifespan of a TBC system can range from 10,000 to 24,000 hours, depending on the application and operating conditions.
The common failure modes of TBCs include erosion, foreign object damage, and buildup of deposits.
The Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD) process is used to deposit ceramic material onto the metal substrate, providing a strong bond and improving the thermal insulation properties of the TBC system.
The typical temperature reduction achieved by using TBCs is around 56-83°C (100-150°F) compared to uncoated components.
TBCs have been used in land-based gas turbines for over 10 years.

The requirements of land-based gas turbines are different from those of aircraft engines, and TBCs must be highly reliable and able to function on all airfoil sections of the first stage vanes and blades.
The Department of Energy's Advanced Turbine System (ATS) program aims to develop a new generation of land-based gas turbine systems with improved efficiency and reduced emissions.
TBCs have been used in industrial gas turbines for over 5 years.
The use of TBCs in industrial gas turbines can increase engine efficiency and performance, but requires reliable and durable coating systems.
